i0: Both tenses talk about the past. The **past simple** (*I lost*) is about a **finished** time. The **present perfect** (*I've lost*) connects the past with **now**.
i1: The most important question is: **do you say or mean a finished time?** If yes, use the past simple. This page goes from that basic rule to the cases where both are possible.
ppps-finished-time.t: Finished time or up to now?
ppps-finished-time.s: Past simple with a **finished time** (*yesterday, last week, in 2019, ago*). Present perfect when there's **no finished time** and the past is connected to now.
ppps-finished-time.b0.h: Past simple (finished time) | Present perfect (up to now / no time given)
ppps-finished-time.b1: Words with a **finished time** take the past simple: *yesterday, last night / week / year, ago, in 2015, on Monday, when I was a child, What time…? When…?*
ppps-finished-time.b2: Words that mean **up to now** often take the present perfect: *ever, never, already, yet, so far, since, for* (up to now).
ppps-finished-time.b3: You can't use the present perfect with a finished time: *I saw him yesterday.* Not *I've seen him yesterday*.
ppps-finished-time.w0: last night is finished: past simple
ppps-finished-time.w2: on Sunday is finished: past simple
ppps-experience-details.t: Have you ever…? Yes, I went there in…
ppps-experience-details.s: Use the present perfect to **ask about or introduce** an experience, then the past simple for the **details** (when, where, how).
ppps-experience-details.b0: Conversations about experiences often start with the present perfect and continue in the past simple:
ppps-experience-details.b2: *B: Yes, I **have**. I **went** there last spring.*
ppps-experience-details.b4: *B: I **loved** it. We **stayed** near the bridge.*
ppps-experience-details.b5: The first question is about life up to now (no time). The follow-up questions are about a **specific** visit, so they use the past simple.
ppps-experience-details.b6: *Have you been…?* asks about the experience. *When did you go?* asks about the details.
ppps-experience-details.w0: Details with a time: past simple.
ppps-experience-details.w1: Details about the match: past simple.
ppps-still-true.s: *I**'ve lived** here for ten years* = I still live here. *I **lived** there for ten years* = I don't now. People who are dead: past simple.
ppps-still-true.b0: With *for* and with situations, the tense tells you if the situation is **still true**:
ppps-still-true.b1.0.0: *He**'s worked** at the bank for five years.* (he still does)
ppps-still-true.b1.0.1: *He **worked** at the bank for five years.* (he doesn't now)
ppps-still-true.b2: When we talk about people who are **no longer alive**, or periods that are over, we use the past simple: *Hafez **wrote** beautiful poetry.* For living people whose work continues, the present perfect is common: *This author **has written** twelve novels* (and may write more).
ppps-still-true.b3: Think about **now**: Is the situation still going on? Can the person still do it? If not, use the past simple.
ppps-still-true.w1: He's no longer alive: past simple.
ppps-this-morning.t: Today, this morning, this year: finished or not?
ppps-this-morning.s: *this morning, today, this week* take the present perfect if the period **isn't over** and the past simple if it **is over**.
ppps-this-morning.b0: Some time phrases can mean a finished or an unfinished period. It depends on **when you are speaking**:
ppps-this-morning.b1.h: Speaking at 10 am | Speaking at 3 pm
ppps-this-morning.b2: With ***today, this week, this month, this year***, the present perfect is the usual choice while the period continues: *It**'s been** a busy week.* At the end of a period, people often use the past simple: *(on Friday evening) It **was** a busy week.*
ppps-this-morning.b3: If you mention a specific time **within** the unfinished period, use the past simple: *I**'ve** spoken to her **today**. I **spoke** to her **at 9**.*
ppps-this-morning.w0: At 9 pm the morning is over.
